Commensal microbiota-coated biohybrid implants induce antibiofilm, osteogenic, and immunomodulatory responses in a human 3D immunocompetent model
Educational impact of a bacteriological training program and field assessment of antimicrobial susceptibility testing among bovine veterinarians in Japan
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health concern, and appropriate antimicrobial use in food-producing animal medicine requires accurate bacteriological diagnosis. However, the effectiveness of bacteriological training and the reliability of in-house antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) in food-animal practice remain unclear. We assessed preliminary organism identification accuracy and the impact of a bacteriological training program among bovine veterinarians affiliated with NOSAI Hokkaido, Japan, and evaluated disk diffusion AST variability using the same Escherichia coli isolate. Preliminary identification accuracy increased from 37% (35/94) before training to 91% (86/94) immediately afterward. Pre-training accuracy was significantly higher among frequent testers than among participants who performed no routine bacteriological testing, whereas post-training accuracy was high across all three testing-frequency groups. In the AST assessment, inhibition zone diameters varied substantially across all six antimicrobial disks, and discordant susceptible/resistant (S/R) interpretations occurred in more than 50% of participants for two agents. Multivariable generalized estimating equation analyses showed that smear technique was significantly associated with discordant S/R interpretations, whereas agar medium was not significantly associated with discordance after adjustment. The association between inoculum quantity and discordance could not be reliably established because only two participants were classified in the appropriate-inoculum category. These findings demonstrate the immediate benefit of structured practical training for improving preliminary organism identification and highlight the need to standardize field-based AST, particularly smear technique. Wider adoption of the simplified disk diffusion procedures described in the national mastitis guidebook may improve AST consistency in clinical practice.

title: Understanding diagnostic challenges and identifying priorities to tackle antimicrobial resistance in conflict zones
abstract: Armed conflict is a key driver of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Diagnostics are critical tools for limiting the impact of AMR where resources are limited. We analyse how conflict shifts the needs and deliverability of AMR diagnostics and identify opportunities to strengthen scope and capacity in these settings with persistent state-delivered health governance and policy. Key priorities include optimisation of robust diagnostic processing, workload and data sharing tools, and procurement policies suitable for resource-limited settings, including linked electronic workload and data-sharing tools with offline options, to support delivery of individual patient care, infection prevention and control, and surveillance.

title: Source Apportionment and Resistome Signatures of Community and Hospital Effluents in Urban Sewer Networks
abstract: Antibiotic resistance surveillance has traditionally focused on clinical settings, potentially overlooking broader microbial reservoirs in the community. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides a powerful tool for capturing these population-level signals. This study aimed to identify source-specific resistome characteristics and estimate the relative compositional contributions of hospital and residential wastewater to the downstream wastewater treatment plant (WWTP). By integrating droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) with metagenomic sequencing, spatiotemporal dynamics across an urban sewer network were characterized. Bacterial 16S rRNA gene concentrations did not differ significantly between hospital and residential wastewater. Under the specified flow scenarios, hospital wastewater represented a small fraction of the estimated total influent volume. Bayesian source tracking further indicated that residential sources collectively accounted for nearly 80% of the inferred source contribution to the influent antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) profile and 70.9% of the influent microbial community composition, whereas hospital wastewater accounted for only 5.5% of the inferred resistome contribution. These findings show that hospital wastewater contained clinically important resistance genes (e.g., blaKPC-2), whereas the sampled residential references accounted for the largest combined inferred contribution to the influent microbiome and resistome. Together, these results highlight the importance of incorporating community surveillance through wastewater-based approaches within the One Health framework.

title: Radical-Mediated integrated sludge treatment Strategy: Simultaneous enhancement of dewatering Performance, attenuation of antibiotic resistance Genes, and sustainable resource reutilization
abstract: This study presents a systematic investigation of the performance, underlying mechanisms, and resource recovery potential of a calcium oxide-activated persulfate (PS/CaO) system for sludge treatment. Following PS/CaO conditioning, sludge dewaterability was markedly enhanced, with the capillary suction time (CST) reduced by 45.5%. This enhancement was primarily through structural disruption of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) and subsequent release of bound water. The PS/CaO process also yielded marked attenuation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), reducing their absolute abundance by over 1.5 log units across all monitored ARG targets. Compositional analysis revealed that sludge organic matter, such as proteins and carbohydrates, underwent progressive degradation and concurrent humification, yielding humic-like and fulvic-like acids at concentrations of 5.7% and 4.2% (w/w), respectively. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) identification confirmed sulfate radicals (SO·) and hydroxyl radicals (·OH) as the dominant reactive species responsible for dissolved organic matter (DOM) transformation with oxygenation, Maillard condensation, and dealkylation identified as key reaction pathways. Pot experiments further demonstrated that application of the treated sludge at a 2% (w/w) dosage significantly increased wheat fresh biomass by 87.83% relative to the control. Life-cycle assessment further confirmed its superior environmental compatibility relative to aerobic composting. This study presents a technically viable approach and a robust theoretical basis for achieving enhanced sludge dewatering, effective risk mitigation, and safe resource reutilization.

title: Beyond the Gut: Genome-Characterised Salmonella Kentucky ST198 Urinary Tract Infection
abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella urinary tract infections (UTIs) are rare and may be linked to immunosuppression, chronic illnesses, or structural urinary tract abnormalities. Salmonella enterica serovar Kentucky (ST198) is a globally disseminated lineage associated with fluoroquinolone resistance and the acquisition of additional antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. This is the first Indian case report of a rare UTI caused by Salmonella Kentucky ST198, resistant to both fluoroquinolones and extended-spectrum cephalosporins. This report emphasises the value of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for serovar-level characterisation and resistance-gene discovery in uncommon Salmonella isolates, as well as the importance of off-label azithromycin use for treating UTI for a favourable outcome.

title: S-layers as functional armours: structure, function and variability in Clostridioides difficile
abstract: Surface layers (S-layers) are paracrystalline protein lattices that serve as molecular exoskeletons and environmental interfaces across diverse bacteria and archaea. Despite their widespread occurrence, S-layers remain comparatively understudied. The available models do not fully represent the structural and physiological diversity of S-layers, and fragmented methodologies limit comprehensive functional comparisons and detailed characterisation. Recently determined high-resolution structural details for multiple variants of Clostridioides difficile S-layer provide a uniquely rich model system with functional links to antimicrobial resistance, phage recognition and immune evasion. In this review, we present C. difficile S-layers as extremely diverse, adaptable and multifunctional structures. We (i) summarise known S-layer roles in C. difficile infection; (ii) present a comprehensive comparison of their extremely diverse structures, including unique features and topological differences in lattice assemblies; (iii) propose quantitative metrics for comparative, structural analysis of these S-layers; (iv) outline S-layer pore size thresholds for the diffusion of metabolites essential for C. difficile growth; and (v) explore possible mechanisms underlying S-layer function and highlight the key outstanding questions.

title: Shifting microbial profiles and antimicrobial susceptibility in infectious keratitis: a 13-year longitudinal analysis at a Brazilian tertiary center
abstract: Infectious keratitis is a sight-threatening disease often managed with empiric antibiotics. Continuous monitoring of causative agents and resistance patterns is essential to detect shifts in susceptibility and optimize treatment protocols. This study analyzed the etiology and antibiotic susceptibility trends of microbial keratitis at a major tertiary referral center over a 13-year period. Retrospective analysis of corneal scrapings from patients clinically diagnosed with infectious keratitis between January 2013 and December 2025. Cases were divided into two periods (2013-2019 and 2020-2025) to evaluate temporal trends. Statistical analyses included Bonferroni-corrected chi-square/Fisher's exact tests and the Cochran-Armitage trend test. Among 649 corneal scrapings, 343 (52.9%) were culture-positive, yielding 420 isolates (18.1% polymicrobial). Bacteria predominated (88.8%), comprising 56.9% Gram-Positive (GP) and 31.9% Gram-Negative (GN) isolates. Coagulase-negative Staphylococci were the most frequent GP (21.4%), while Pseudomonas aeruginosa (11.4%) was the leading GN. Fungi comprised for 10.2%. Longitudinal analysis revealed significant reductions in Cutibacterium acnes (adjusted p < 0.001) and Serratia marcescens (adjusted p = 0.009), a downward trend in fungal isolation (p = 0.010) and a marginal decline in ciprofloxacin susceptibility among GN (p = 0.056). All GP isolates demonstrated 100% in vitro susceptibility to vancomycin. Methicillin resistance was identified in 19.4% of S. aureus and 43.1% of coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The microbiological profile of infectious keratitis showed significant temporal shifts, including a reduction in C. acnes and a downward trend in fungal isolation. While Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms maintained high susceptibility to vancomycin and amikacin, respectively, a marginal, non-statistically-significant decline in ciprofloxacin susceptibility among Gram-negative isolates warrants continuous microbiological surveillance.

title: Persistent pharmaceuticals and their transformation Products: From persistence mechanisms to AI-assisted integrated treatment for safe water reuse
abstract: This review examines the physicochemical mechanisms governing pharmaceutical persistence, the formation of transformation products (TPs), and the effectiveness and limitations of conventional and advanced treatment technologies for water reuse, focusing on carbamazepine, diclofenac, iodinated contrast media, metformin, and selected antibiotics, which persist through wastewater treatment. The review follows one chain of reasoning: persistence drivers determine which TPs form, which compartments and exposure pathways are reached, and which treatment barriers can act. Conventional activated sludge often provides incomplete removal, whereas integrated trains combining biological processes, adsorption, ozonation, UV/HO, membranes, and other advanced oxidation technologies can improve control, although energy demand, membrane fouling, residuals, and TP formation remain constraints. Pilot- and full-scale studies report average abatement of about 80% or more with ozonation or activated carbon, but behavior differs among compounds, and evidence for complete multi-barrier trains is limited. Unlike reviews addressing occurrence, individual technologies, or TPs separately, this review links the drivers of persistence to the selection and sequencing of treatment barriers, and extends the assessment to groundwater migration, soil-plant and food-chain transfer, and antimicrobial-resistance pathways within a common water-reuse framework. This supports adaptive treatment design targeting parent compounds, TPs, and cross-compartment risks. HRMS, non-target screening, and AI/ML-assisted optimization support adaptive monitoring and control. However, identifying a TP does not demonstrate risk, so effect-based methods are needed, and AI/ML applications are mainly predictive and validated on small datasets. Safe and sustainable water reuse likely requires multi-barrier treatment, source control, continuous monitoring, TP assessment, and integrated risk management.

title: Green synthesis of Brassica rapa-mediated magnesium oxide nanoparticles MgO NPs with ROS-driven antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria
abstract: The ability of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria to develop antibiotic-resistant biofilms enables their ongoing survival in various environments. In this study, MgO NPs were synthesized using an environmentally sustainable green method mediated by Brassica rapa. The antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of the synthesized MgO nanoparticles were evaluated against clinical isolates of A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, and E. coli. These nanoparticles were checked for their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities by broth microdilution assay and microtiter plate assay. The biogenic MgO NPs exhibited strong antibacterial activity with an MIC of 125-250 µg/ml and bactericidal effects at 500-1000 µg /ml. Planktonic growth inhibition exceeded 90% at 50 µg/ml after 48 h and reached 99% at 100 µg/ml after 72 h. Biofilm formation was suppressed by 60-90% at 50 µg/ml while pre-established biofilms were reduced by 97-99% following prolonged exposure. Mechanistic studies demonstrated substantial destruction of extracellular polymeric substances. Specifically, proteins decreased by 68%, carbohydrates by 55%, and extracellular DNA by 33%, while intracellular reactive oxygen species simultaneously increased by 2-3 times. The results demonstrate that Brassica rapa-derived MgO NPs function as effective, sustainable nanomaterial that prevents biofilm formation by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens.

title: Insects as a Novel Source of Antimicrobial Therapeutics: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
abstract: The widespread misuse and overuse of antibiotics over recent decades have contributed to the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), creating a growing need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. Insects are a rich yet underutilized source of antimicrobial compounds, particularly antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), which play a crucial role in their innate immune systems. Although previous reviews have discussed insect-derived AMPs and bioactive compounds, relatively few have comprehensively examined their activities against bacterial, fungal, and viral pathogens. This review highlights recent advances in insect-derived AMPs, focusing on their diversity across insect groups, antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral activities, mechanisms of action, and therapeutic potential in the context of AMR. We also discuss other insect-derived products with antimicrobial properties, including venom components, wound-associated secretions, and chitin-derived biomaterials. In addition, we examine the potential of combining insect-derived AMPs with conventional antimicrobials, which may enhance antimicrobial efficacy, reduce the required dose of conventional agents, and potentially limit the emergence of resistance. Emerging omics- and AI-based approaches for identifying and characterizing promising antimicrobial candidates are considered, alongside a discussion of key challenges associated with their therapeutic application. Overall, insect-derived AMPs show great promise as alternative or complementary antimicrobial agents; however, further clinical studies are required to establish their therapeutic relevance.

title: IgY-Based Immunotherapy Against MDR/XDR/PDR Bacterial Infections: Mechanisms and Experimental Evidence From In Vitro and In Vivo Studies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the greatest threats to global public health, largely driven by the rapid dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) bacterial pathogens. The limited antibacterial pipeline, together with the declining effectiveness of conventional antibiotics, highlights the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Among emerging immunotherapeutic approaches, immunoglobulin Y (IgY), the principal antibody found in egg yolk, has attracted increasing attention because of its high specificity, favorable safety profile, ethical and scalable production, and low propensity to promote antimicrobial resistance. Experimental evidence consistently demonstrates that pathogen-specific IgY exhibits potent antibacterial activity against priority MDR pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Salmonella enterica. Across multiple in vitro and animal studies, IgY reduced bacterial burden, inhibited biofilm formation and bacterial motility, enhanced opsonophagocytic clearance, attenuated inflammatory responses, improved survival, and frequently restored or potentiated the activity of conventional antibiotics. Recent advances in inhalable formulations, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, and combination therapies further expand the translational potential of IgY for managing difficult-to-treat bacterial infections. Therefore, current evidence supports IgY as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy that may complement conventional antimicrobial therapy and, in selected settings, potentially serve as an alternative to antibiotics. Although encouraging preclinical findings have accumulated, additional well-designed clinical trials, standardized manufacturing protocols, and optimized delivery platforms are essential to define the clinical settings in which IgY can safely and effectively be used alone or alongside conventional antimicrobial therapy.

title: Autologous Conditioned Serum Improves Early Wound Healing Scores of Postextraction Dental Wound in Dogs
abstract: This retrospective study evaluated the potential role of autologous conditioned serum (ACS) as an adjunctive therapy to improve postextraction dental wound healing in dogs. Clinical records of 40 dogs that underwent tooth extraction were included in the analysis. Data from 20 dogs that had received ACS applied to the extraction site following suturing were compared with those from 20 dogs that received the standard treatment. Healing outcomes were assessed from follow-up notes at days 3, 7 and 14, using the Early Wound Healing Score (EHS) to evaluate haemostasis, inflammation, and wound margin closure. Analysis revealed that dogs treated with ACS demonstrated significantly higher EHS compared to controls. By day 3, the ACS group showed a significant improvement in EHS compared to controls ( = .01), with a large effect size (Hedges = 0.87). The higher clinical scores persisted at day 7, with a significantly higher score for clinical signs of reepithelialization in the ACS group (  .02, Hedges  0.78). These differences were observed across subgroups, regardless of patient demographics or clinical presentation within the study population. The findings suggest that ACS is associated with improved EHS, including reepithelialization and haemostasis scores.

title: Toxin-responsive metal-organic framework nanocarriers for precision delivery of antimicrobial peptides against drug-resistant infections
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance has emerged as a major global healthcare challenge owing to the rapid rise in multidrug-resistant bacterial infections and the declining effectiveness of conventional antibiotics. Antimicrobial peptides have gained considerable attention as alternative therapeutic agents because of their broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, membrane-targeting mechanisms, immunomodulatory functions, and reduced susceptibility to resistance development. The clinical translation of antimicrobial peptides is limited by enzymatic degradation, poor stability, rapid clearance, systemic toxicity, and inefficient infection site targeting. In this context, metal-organic frameworks have emerged as effective nanocarriers for precision antimicrobial peptide delivery owing to their tunable porosity, high loading capacity, surface functionalization, and stimuli-responsive behavior. This review comprehensively discusses the molecular mechanisms of antimicrobial peptides, engineering strategies for metal-organic framework-based delivery systems, and toxin-responsive nanocarrier designs for selective antimicrobial therapy. Different toxin-responsive approaches, including lipid bilayer-disruptable systems, membrane-coated toxin-decoy metal-organic frameworks, phospholipase-triggered platforms, virulence-factor-amplified systems, and dual-responsive nanocarriers, are highlighted for their ability to achieve site-specific antimicrobial peptide release in pathogen-rich microenvironments. Furthermore, recent,, and preclinical studies demonstrating therapeutic efficacy against multidrug-resistant and biofilm-associated infections are reviewed. Toxin-responsive metal-organic framework nanocarriers represent an advanced precision nanomedicine strategy with considerable potential for combating drug-resistant bacterial infections.

title: Asymptomatic extragenital Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection among transgender women in Argentina: Prevalence, antimicrobial susceptibility, and molecular characterization
abstract: BackgroundAsymptomatic extragenital(NG) infection contributes to ongoing transmission and may facilitate the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. This study aimed to determine NG prevalence, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, and sequence types among transgender women (TGW).MethodsReal-time PCR (qPCR) and culture for NG were performed on pharyngeal and rectal swabs and first-void urine (FVU) samples from TGW attending Fundación Huésped in Buenos Aires, Argentina (August 2021-March 2022).(Cq) values from qPCR-positive samples were used as a proxy for bacterial load. Culture-positive isolates underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing and NG multi-antigen sequence typing (NG-MAST). Participants were also tested for other sexually transmitted infections (STI) and sociodemographic and behavioral data were collected by questionnaire.ResultsWe included 117 TGW: median age 32 (IQR 29-39), 55% had not completed high school, 54% were currently engaged in sex work, 55% had ≥ 5 sexual partners in the last month, and 68% reported recreational substance use in the previous year. At baseline, 46% were living with HIV, 20% had active syphilis, and 6% extragenital chlamydia. Global NG prevalence (determined by positive qPCR) was 9% (10/117) with 9 rectal infections (8%; 9/116), one pharyngeal infection (1%; 1/117), and none detected in FVU. Only three of nine PCR-positive rectal samples yielded a positive culture. All isolates were susceptible to ceftriaxone and azithromycin and showed intermediate susceptibility or resistance to tetracycline. Sequence types (ST) were ST21119, ST8202, and ST21122. No associations were found between asymptomatic extragenital NG infection and sociodemographic/behavioral factors. Seventy percent of positive PCR samples had a Cq ≥ 28, suggesting lower bacterial loads.ConclusionAsymptomatic extragenital NG infection prevalence among TGW in Buenos Aires was 9%, with no infections detected in FVU, underscoring the importance of extragenital screening. Limited culture recovery highlights the potential value of complementary approaches to antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Niosomal delivery of cefoxitin enhances antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria
abstract: The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections is a serious threat to human health. Biofilm formation and limited antibiotic penetration reduce the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics, highlighting the need for more effective drug-delivery strategies. Niosomes, as promising vesicular drug delivery systems, have shown potential to enhance antibiotic efficacy. This study aimed to encapsulate cefoxitin in niosomes and evaluate its antibacterial effect against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter baumannii, Staphylococcus aureus, and Listeria monocytogenes. Cefoxitin-loaded niosomes were prepared by thin-layer hydration. Physicochemical properties were characterized by dynamic light scattering (DLS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The antibacterial and anti-biofilm activities of free cefoxitin and cefoxitin-loaded niosomes were investigated using microdilution and microtiter plate assays, respectively. Time-kill kinetics were further performed to evaluate bacterial killing kinetics. The findings showed the synthesized niosomes were spherical with a size of 142.3 nm. The release of cefoxitin from niosomes was 62.69% during 72 h, while nearly complete release of free cefoxitin occurred within the same period. Notably, antibacterial investigations revealed that although free cefoxitin showed little effect on Gram-negative bacteria at the concentrations studied, niosomal cefoxitin significantly inhibited their bacterial growth and biofilm formation. Additionally, niosomal cefoxitin enhanced antibacterial and antibiofilm activity compared with free cefoxitin against Gram-positive bacteria. The 72-h time-kill assay showed that niosomal cefoxitin reduced bacterial viability at all time points. The results demonstrate that niosomal delivery enhances the antibacterial activity of cefoxitin and improves its effectiveness against biofilm-forming bacteria.

title: Clinical development of human vaccine candidates against Shigella flexneri: a systematic review of clinical trials
Development of cinnamyl derivatives as antibiotic-potentiating agents
abstract: Here, we report the discovery and optimization of 1-cinnamylpiperazine derivatives as antibiotic-potentiating agents inspired by the known RND efflux pump inhibitor 1-(1-naphthylmethyl)piperazine (NMP). A structurally diverse series of analogues was synthesized and evaluated for intrinsic antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity, and ability to potentiate antibiotic activity against Escherichia coli. Most derivatives showed low intrinsic antibacterial activity, consistent with an adjuvant mode of action. In combination assays, several compounds enhanced the antibiotic activity of erythromycin and linezolid, with halogenated derivatives showing the strongest potentiating effects. Compound 27 displayed the broadest potentiation profile, showing synergistic interactions with five of the seven tested antibiotics, namely linezolid, novobiocin, fusidic acid, pyridomycin, and clindamycin. Notably, it showed a superior potency to the structurally related reference inhibitor NMP. Experiments with AcrAB-TolC-deficient E. coli mutants, together with dye accumulation (Hoechst 33342) and membrane-permeabilization assays, suggested that 1-cinnamylpiperazine derivatives modulate efflux-associated resistance in a manner distinct from NMP, with increased membrane permeability likely contributing to their overall potentiating effect. Beyond planktonic cultures, compound 27 also potentiated erythromycin and linezolid against mature E. coli biofilms. These findings identify 1-cinnamylpiperazines as promising antibiotic adjuvant scaffolds for further optimization against drug-resistant Gram-negative infections.

title: Plasmid-mediated copper resistance in Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. perforans: determination of plasmid copy number and stability
abstract: The management of bacterial spot of tomato is challenged by the widespread occurrence of copper resistance among its causal pathogens. Inpv., a major causal agent, copper resistance is conferred bygenes organized in an operon located on either the chromosome or plasmid. In the United States, copper resistance is predominantly chromosomally encoded. Plasmid-borne resistance is limited to a few phylogenetic groups but is prevalent in other bacterial spot pathogens. We hypothesized that plasmid-encoded copper resistance genes exhibit higher expression than chromosomally encoded genes but may be unstable in the absence of selective pressure for resistance. To test this hypothesis, we examined how the chromosomal versus plasmid-borneoperon influences gene copy number and expression, as well as plasmid stability. Relative to strains with only chromosomal resistance, strains carrying plasmid-encoded resistance exhibited an increased copy number of, a key gene in the operon, while strains carrying both chromosomal and plasmid-encoded resistance showed an even greater increase in gene copy number. Correspondingly,expression was elevated in both groups. Duringgrowth without copper, partial or complete plasmid loss occurred in a subset of strains, and genome sequencing of colonies with reduced plasmid size revealed transposase-mediated plasmid rearrangements. These findings demonstrate that plasmid-borne copper resistance increases gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes but can be unstable without copper selection in some strain backgrounds, highlighting the role of mobile genetic elements in shapingpv.adaptation to changing copper environments.IMPORTANCEPlasmids are key players in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance. Although copper resistance is widespread amongpv.strains, copper-based bactericides remain at the forefront of disease management. We previously demonstrated that distinct genetic elements, including plasmid- and chromosomally encoded genomic islands, contribute to the acquisition of copper resistance and the occurrence of multicopy resistance inpv.. Here, we show that the localization of copper resistance genes on a plasmid, chromosome, or both influences gene copy number and expression of copper resistance genes. Furthermore, rearrangements between co-resident plasmids affect plasmid stability, leading to the loss of copper resistance inpv.. These findings highlight how plasmid dynamics can shape bacterial evolvability and adaptation to selective environments.

title: A global genomic analysis of Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus reveals clade-specific pathogenic and antimicrobial resistance profiles with several mobile genetic elements as key adaptive drivers
abstract: subsp.() is a zoonotic pathogen affecting various mammals, yet its genomic epidemiology remains poorly understood. To address this, we analyzed 428strains from six countries (1993-2024). The whole-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) revealed four clades, with genetic diversity driven by lineage rather than host species or geographic origin. The findings support the conclusion thatis a host generalist, with horses serving as the primary host. The identified virulence-associated genes (VAGs) showed clade-specific distribution patterns: clade 1 lacked adherence factor genes, clade 2 was enriched for the IgG-degrading enzyme gene, and clade 4 was enriched for a specific allele of the virulence-associated coupling protein gene. Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) were detected in 18.2% of strains, and no multidrug resistance was found. ARG prevalence was associated with clade 4, with tetracycline resistance being the most common. Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are pivotal in shaping the accessory genome profiles: prophages function as the primary carriers of exotoxin genes, while integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) serve as the main vehicles for ARGs. Notably, the co-localization of the invasion-associatedallele and ARGs was identified on ICE1, predominantly in clade 4 isolates. In conclusion, the pathogenic potential and resistance profiles ofare shaped by specific evolutionary lineages driven by MGEs. These elements act not only as genetic cargo but also as drivers that provide the conjugative machinery to co-disseminate virulence and resistance traits, accelerating the evolution of zoonotic lineages.IMPORTANCEis an opportunistic pathogen capable of infecting a wide range of hosts, including humans, often causing severe diseases. This study provides a framework for understanding the evolution of, highlighting that its pathogenic potential and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles are shaped by specific MGE-driven evolutionary lineages. The co-localization of the invasion-associatedallele and ARGs on ICEs indicates that these elements provide both the pathogenic advantage and the conjugative machinery required for horizontal spread in. This suggests that antibiotic selection can promote the transmission of virulentlineages. These findings underscore the need for integrated surveillance strategies to monitor both virulence and AMR traits inwithin equine populations to benefit public health.

title: A plasmid-encoded H-NS protein selectively binds its own plasmid
abstract: H-NS is an abundant nucleoid-associated protein found inspecies. Some conjugative plasmids encode H-NS homologs, which are thought to facilitate plasmid maintenance and reduce the fitness costs associated with plasmid carriage. Here, we characterize HppX, an H-NS homolog encoded by the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 of. Our data indicate that HppXhas a strong preference for binding pCROD2 over the chromosome, or other plasmids. By contrast, chromosomally encoded H-NS displays no preference for plasmid sequence. When expressed from a heterologous plasmid in, HppXshowed similar DNA-sequence preference to chromosomally encoded H-NS. Moreover, HppXbinding to a sequence from pCROD2 was much lower when that sequence was cloned in a laboratory plasmid. Thus, HppXpreferentially binds DNA in the context of the plasmid where it is encoded, a phenomenon we term "cognate plasmid specificity." We propose that cognate plasmid specificity occurs through recognition of plasmid-specific DNA topology generated by plasmid-encoded topoisomerases. Cognate plasmid specificity may insulate regulation of plasmid genes from the effects of host DNA, while minimizing disruption of host chromosome regulation due to plasmid carriage.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria carry conjugative plasmids, mobile DNA molecules that spread traits such as antibiotic resistance. Some conjugative plasmids encode proteins related to the bacterial DNA-binding protein H-NS. We show that an H-NS-like protein from the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 binds almost exclusively to the plasmid from which it originates, while largely ignoring the host chromosome. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism that allows plasmids to regulate their own genes with high specificity while minimizing interference with host gene expression.

title: Prevalence of Antimicrobial Resistant Mycoplasma genitalium among Men Who Have Sex with Men: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) is an emerging sexually transmitted pathogen with increasing antimicrobial resistance, and is now a common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). Men who have sex with men (MSM) are at increased risk of sexually transmitted infections, including MG. This systematic review aims to summarize the evidence on the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant MG among MSM. We searched PubMed, Embase, and Scopus from database inception to January 31, 2026 for studies that reported the prevalence of macrolide, fluoroquinolone, or tetracycline-resistant MG among MSM, included studies according to pre-determined eligibility criteria, and conducted a random effects meta-analysis to summarize findings and assess for trends over time and differences across geographic regions. Study quality was assessed using a 10-item critical appraisal tool developed by the Joanna Briggs Institute specifically for prevalence studies. Fifty-one studies (N = 5,247) were included that conducted MG resistance testing, with sample sizes ranging from 7 to 1557 (median 56). The pooled prevalence of macrolide resistance was 75.7% (95% CI 69.5%-81.5%) and that of fluoroquinolone resistance was 23.5% (95% CI 17.8%-29.7%). Studies were highly heterogeneous (I2 = 94.5% for macrolide resistance and 89.1% for fluoroquinolone resistance). Most studies were of low to moderate quality per the assessment tool. This systematic review revealed a high prevalence of macrolide resistant MG among MSM, and a lower, but significant prevalence of fluoroquinolone resistance. Larger, more rigorous studies that focus exclusively on MSM are needed to better estimate the global burden of antimicrobial resistant MG among MSM.

title: Antibiotic Resistance in India Over a Decade: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Clinical and Molecular Evidence (2015-2025)
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a major global public health threat that compromises the effectiveness of antibiotic agents and increases morbidity, mortality, and health care costs. India faces a substantial AMR burden driven by high infectious disease prevalence, widespread antibiotic use, and variable surveillance capacity. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence on antibiotic resistance patterns in India from 2015 to 2025, estimate the prevalence of resistance among major bacterial pathogens, evaluate molecular resistance determinants, and assess mortality associated with resistant infections. A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, surveillance reports, and grey literature was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies reporting antibiotic resistance data from India between January 2015 and December 2025 were included. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by 2 reviewers. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of antibiotic resistance, molecular determinants of resistance, and mortality outcomes, and heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q and I2 statistics. Forty-six studies met the inclusion criteria. The pooled prevalence of antibiotic resistance was 55.7% (95% CI: 47.4%-63.9%; I2=98.6%). High resistance rates were reported among major gram-negative pathogens, particularly Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Molecular meta-analysis demonstrated a pooled prevalence of resistance-associated genes of 64.5% (95% CI: 46.0%-83.0%), with blaNDM, blaOXA-48-like, and blaKPC being the most frequently reported determinants. Mortality associated with resistant infections was 31.0% (95% CI: 18.2%-43.8%). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across all analyses. Available evidence indicates that antibiotic resistance remains a significant health care challenge in India. High levels of multidrug resistance, widespread dissemination of carbapenemase genes, and considerable mortality associated with resistant infections underscore the need for strengthened antibiotic stewardship, standardized surveillance, expanded molecular diagnostics, and coordinated public health interventions. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity and the predominance of studies from tertiary-care settings. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261406324).

title: Co-occurrence of bla(NDM-5) and mcr-1 on Two Distinct, Independently Transferable Plasmids in Commensal Escherichia coli ST156 from a Healthy Companion Dog
abstract: The emergence of carbapenem- and colistin-resistant Enterobacterales mediated by transmissible plasmids poses a critical One Health threat by compromising the efficacy of last-resort antimicrobials. We characterized a commensalST156 isolate recovered from a clinically healthy companion dog in South Korea that carriedandon distinct plasmids. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed a multidrug-resistant phenotype, including resistance to carbapenems (imipenem MIC, ≥8 μg/mL) and colistin (MIC, 8 μg/mL). Hybrid long- and short-read genome assembly localizedto an IncX3 plasmid andto an IncX4 plasmid. Broth-mating assays showed that each plasmid was independently transferable under the corresponding single-antimicrobial selection. Among 30 transconjugant colonies screened under each selection, both resistance determinants were detected in five colistin-selected and two meropenem-selected colonies, indicating co-detection of both resistance determinants in a minority of the screened colonies. Comparative genomic analysis showed that the IncX4-plasmid shared a highly conserved backbone with globally distributed IncX4 plasmids from diverse sources. These findings demonstrate asymptomatic carriage of independently transferable carbapenem- and colistin-resistance plasmids in a companion animal and support the inclusion of companion animals in integrated antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Magnetic Resonance Reveals Radical Stability in Native Biofilms and Its Role in Bacterial Resistance
abstract: Bacterial cells embedded in biofilms exhibit enhanced antimicrobial resistance compared with planktonic cells, contributing to persistent infections and failure of conventional antibiotic treatments. This resistance is influenced by the extracellular matrix (ECM), a heterogeneous network of polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids surrounding embedded cells. However, how the ECM regulates the accessibility of redox-active small molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we combine electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), solid-state NMR (ssNMR), and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) ssNMR to determine how native Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf0-1 colony biofilms differentially reduce nitroxide radicals across morphologies. EPR reveals that radical reduction depends on biofilm morphology, hydration, and ECM composition. Wild-type biofilms exhibit slower nitroxide reduction than planktonic cells, while isolated ECM and dehydrated biofilms show negligible reduction, highlighting the importance of cellular accessibility. ssNMR identifies preferential spatial proximity of nitroxides to ECM polysaccharides and lipids, while DNP ssNMR reveals increasing polysaccharide content across biofilm morphologies that correlates with slower reduction kinetics. These findings support a model of protection in which the ECM provides the barrier to nitroxide access, and cellular reduction is the final step. Our integrated magnetic resonance approach provides molecular insight into how biofilm composition and structure determine the fate of therapeutically relevant redox-active small molecules.

title: Molecular Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Patterns of Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative Bacilli Isolated from Intensive Care Unit Patients in a Tertiary Care Hospital
abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacilli (GNB) present a critical challenge in intensive care units (ICUs), severely limiting therapeutic options. This study evaluated the prevalence and molecular resistance mechanisms of GNB in ICU patients. Hospital-acquired urinary tract infections are among the most common healthcare-associated infections in ICUs. The emergence of MDR Gram-negative bacilli has reduced available treatment options and increased morbidity. This study aimed to evaluate antimicrobial resistance patterns and characterize major resistance genes among Gram-negative bacilli isolated from ICU patients. A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from 2019 to 2022 across two tertiary centers in North India. We analyzed 427 non-duplicate MDR GNB isolates from ICU urinary samples. Identification followed standard biochemical protocols. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed through Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion as per Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. Phenotypic detection of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL), AmpC, and carbapenemase production was performed, alongside molecular characterization of resistance genes (blaTEM, blaSHV, blaCTX-M, blaNDM, blaIMP, blaVIM, blaOXA). In the present study, most isolates originated from the medical ICU (66.0%). Most MDR GNB isolates were from males (52%), and the majority of patients belonged to the age group > 60 years. The predominant isolates were Escherichia coli (60%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (19%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (12%). Alarmingly high resistance rates to Cephalosporins (>90%), Fluoroquinolones (>80%), and Carbapenems (70% overall) were observed. Overall, 40.9% of isolates were ESBL producers, 24.82% AmpC producers, and 13.81% Carbapenemase producers. Molecular analysis revealed a high prevalence of blaCTX M (100%), blaVIM (66%), and blaNDM (48%). The high prevalence of diverse resistance mechanisms underscores the impact of indiscriminate antimicrobial use. Implementation of stringent antimicrobial stewardship and robust infection control practices is essential to mitigate the spread of MDR pathogens in critical care settings.

title: Clonal, regionally clustered spread-rather than vertical transmission-explains surges in fluoroquinolone‑resistant Campylobacter jejuni in Finnish broilers
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni is a major zoonotic foodborne pathogen, with poultry recognized as an important reservoir for human infection. Although antimicrobial use in Finnish broiler production is minimal, sporadic increases in fluoroquinolone- and tetracycline-resistant C. jejuni have been detected. We investigated the population structure, antimicrobial resistance, and transmission pathways of C. jejuni in Finnish poultry production. A total of 333 C. jejuni isolates collected from breeder (n = 145) and broiler (n = 188) flocks during 2014-2019 were characterized using whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial resistance profiling, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), core-genome MLST (cgMLST), and phylogenomic analysis. Resistance to fluoroquinolones and tetracycline was concentrated in specific years and was strongly associated with particular lineages, especially ST-206 clonal complex (CC), whereas the predominant ST-45 CC was largely susceptible. Genomic clustering identified several resistant clones circulating among geographically proximate broiler farms, indicating regional horizontal dissemination. Resistant isolates from breeders were uncommon, and no genomic evidence supported vertical transmission of resistant strains from breeder to broiler flocks. Instead, resistance peaks were primarily attributable to clonal expansion of successful resistant lineages. Transient increases in fluoroquinolone- and tetracycline-resistant C. jejuni in Finnish broiler production were driven mainly by regional clonal horizontal spread rather than vertical transmission from breeders to broilers. These findings highlight the value of genomic surveillance for detecting and tracking antimicrobial-resistant Campylobacter lineages and support the integration of molecular epidemiology into poultry surveillance and control programmes.

title: FibriLysins disrupt Staphylococcus aureus biofilms and abscess communities
abstract: The rise of antibiotic resistance, particularly among pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, necessitates innovative antibacterial strategies. Here we introduce FibriLysins, a class of engineered enzymes combining staphylokinase and endolysin, which dismantle fibrin-encapsulated multicellular staphylococcal communities, including biofilms and staphylococcal abscess communities (SACs). We characterized diverse staphylokinases, developing a library of 27 FibriLysins, with a 78% positive hit rate. The lead variant, FL-028, has significant antibacterial activity against prevalent clinical S. aureus isolates. In vitro, FL-028 reduced bacterial counts in SACs by 3.4 log and in biofilms by 2.3 log. In vivo, FL-028 exhibits superior efficacy in a mouse model of bone fracture-related infection, outperforming vancomycin by 1 log and eliminating SAC presence in tissues. FL-028 shows no adverse effects on bone healing, as confirmed by histological examination, mechanical testing and micro-computed tomography analyses. These preclinical findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins as a robust and safe therapeutic approach against difficult-to-treat staphylococcal infections.

title: Metagenomic Insights into Microplastic Micro-interfaces: Transforming Pollutants and Spreading Resistance
abstract: Microplastic micro-interfaces (MPMI) in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) serve as critical hubs for microbial colonization, pollutant transformation, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dissemination. In this study, a large-scale genome-resolved metagenomic approach was employed to reconstruct 463 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from biofilms established on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), and polypropylene (PP) within a municipal WWTP. Taxonomic profiling revealed that MPMI selectively enriched strict anaerobes and uncultured taxa, driving a profound ecological shift from the surrounding water and indicating the formation of localized hypoxic micro-niches. Functionally, the MPMI microbiome constructed a highly integrated metabolic network. Key dominant lineages were found to synergistically couple aromatic hydrocarbon degradation (via the shikimate pathway and β-oxidation) with complex carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling, while deploying energy-efficient nucleotide salvage strategies to ensure biofilm stabilization under nutrient stress. Crucially, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) emerged as a fundamental mechanism for functional diversification, facilitating the active cross-genomic exchange of key adaptive traits associated with pollutant metabolism and biofilm regulation. Furthermore, MPMI harbored a highly diverse resistome comprising 36 ARG categories and 289 subtypes, highlighted by the critical genomic co-localization of mobile elements and clinical resistance markers (e.g., mcr-5.1, mupA) in core colonizers. Ultimately, these genomic insights elucidate the MPMI as a profound ecological hotspot driving the concurrent adaptation of metabolic networks and the resistome, thereby exacerbating the risks of ARG dissemination in aquatic environments.

title: Recasting Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Through Contemporary Analytical Frameworks: An Integrated Analysis Using the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024 and AWaRe Classification in a Tertiary Care Hospital of Saurashtra, Western India
abstract: Indian antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance rarely uses contemporary global frameworks, and Saurashtra is under-represented in the national evidence base. We applied the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List (BPPL) 2024 and the WHO AWaRe (Access-Watch-Reserve) classification to institutional surveillance data, with national and global benchmarking. Cross-sectional analysis of 2,195 non-duplicate clinical bacterial isolates (May-October 2024) at a 1,200-bed government tertiary care teaching hospital. Susceptibility testing followed CLSI M100-S33 (VITEK 2 Compact; Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion); multi-drug resistance (MDR) followed Magiorakos criteria. Isolates were assigned to BPPL 2024 tiers by resistant phenotype, and agent-level resistance was grouped by AWaRe 2023 category. MDR correlates were explored by multivariable logistic regression. The isolate was the unit of analysis; proportions describe cultured isolates, not infections or patients. Isolates meeting Critical-priority phenotypes numbered 1,192 (54.3% of the isolate pool): third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (n = 1,086; 49.5%; ceftriaxone resistance 78% in E. coli and 61% in K. pneumoniae) and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (n = 106; 4.8%). High-priority phenotypes accounted for at most 228 isolates (10.4%). Within the Access group, Enterobacterales resistance was high to ampicillin (89.7% in E. coli) and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (77-83%) but lower to gentamicin (22-33%); Watch-group fluoroquinolone resistance was 47-73%. Meropenem resistance in E. coli (1%) and K. pneumoniae (7%) was markedly lower than ICMR AMRSN 2023 national estimates (40% and 54%). MDR was present in 58.6% of isolates and was independently associated with ICU admission, age >60 years, tracheal-aspirate specimens, and surgical-department admission. Reading isolate-level surveillance data through the BPPL 2024 and AWaRe frameworks adds a priority- and stewardship-oriented layer to the conventional antibiogram. These proportions describe cultured isolates, not the frequency of resistant infection in patients. The low Enterobacterales carbapenem resistance relative to national benchmarks warrants multi-center, consumption-linked confirmation.

title: Tissue-Site Distribution, Antimicrobial Resistance Profile, and Phenotypic ESBL Production of Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Chicken Carcasses in Bharatpur Metropolitan City, Chitwan, Nepal
abstract: Poultry meat is Nepal's most dynamic agricultural subsector, yet food safety remains a concern as retail carcasses are frequently contaminated by antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli. This cross-sectional study determined the tissue-site distribution, antimicrobial resistance profile, and phenotypic ESBL production of phenotypically identified E. coli isolated from 144 retail chicken carcasses collected from 16 randomly selected meat shops (9 carcasses per shop) in Bharatpur Metropolitan City, Chitwan, Nepal, sampling the liver, muscle, and skin of each bird. Of 432 tissue samples examined, 96 E. coli isolates were recovered, giving an overall tissue-level prevalence of 22.22% and a carcass-level prevalence of 40.97% (59/144; shop-cluster-adjusted 95% CI 29.4-53.6%). Isolation was highest from liver (34.72%), followed by muscle (21.53%) and skin (10.42%); the odds of isolation were 4.17 times higher in the liver than in muscle and 12.67 times higher in the liver than in skin (p<0.001). Susceptibility testing against seven antibiotics showed the highest resistance to nalidixic acid (82.29%) and tetracycline (71.88%), and the lowest resistance to ceftriaxone (12.50%). Multidrug resistance was detected in 91.67% (88/96; 95% CI 84.24-96.33%) extensive drug resistance in 59.38% (57/96; 95% CI: 48.87-69.29%) and pan drug resistance in 2.08% (2/96; 95% CI: 0.25-7.32%) of isolates, with a mean MAR index of 0.63 ± 0.17, highest among liver isolates (0.68 ± 0.16). Phenotypic ESBL positivity by the combined disk test was observed in 18.75% (18/96) of isolates, most frequently from the liver (22%). As identification relied on phenotypic method without molecular or virulence confirmation, these findings indicate that poultry may serve as a reservoir of phenotypically antimicrobial-resistant E. coli, with the liver showing the highest contamination and resistance burden, underscoring the need for targeted surveillance along Nepal's poultry supply chain.

title: Collateral Sensitivity in Bacteria: Phenomenon, Mechanisms, Modulators and Therapeutic Prospects
abstract: The rapid proliferation and infection of multidrug-resistant bacteria pose a significant threat to global public health. The gradual increase in drug resistance, primarily driven by the inappropriate use of antibiotics, underscores the urgent need for developing novel therapeutic approaches for drug-resistant bacterial infections. Collateral sensitivity (CS) describes the phenomenon whereby bacteria resistance to a specific antibiotic increases susceptibility to other antibiotics. In some cases of antibiotic resistance, CS can provide rapid and effective guidance for clinical drug use by detecting the lowest drug sensitivity concentration of resistant bacteria. In order to prevent or mitigate the emergence of drug-resistant bacteria, it is crucial to thoroughly investigate the underlying mechanisms of CS. This article discusses recent research progress on the CS phenomenon, its mechanisms, influencing factors, and the therapeutic potential of CS in bacteria.

title: erm(46) copy number determines macrolide resistance in Rhodococcus equi
abstract: To develop a multiplex real-time PCR assay for simultaneous detection of Rhodococcus equi (choE), virulence (vapA), and macrolide-resistance determinants (erm[46], erm[51]), and evaluate their clinical and temporal trends. Clinical R equi isolates (n = 229) obtained from the Hagyard Equine Medical Institute laboratory were collected sequentially over a 3-year surveillance period (2021 to 2023) from 14 states and underwent broth microdilution susceptibility testing. A cohort of 214 isolates with high-quality DNA was characterized using quantitative PCR. Geographic distribution, seasonal trends, and genotypic-phenotypic concordance were evaluated. The multiplex PCR assay demonstrated 100% analytical specificity. The virulence gene vapA was present in 94.4% (202 of 214) of isolates. The macrolide resistance determinant erm(46) was highly prevalent at 62.6% (134 of 214), showing a significant seasonal increase during July to December periods at 76.6% (vs 58.2% in January to June). Crucially, erm(51) was detected in a single isolate (0.5%), representing its first recorded clinical identification in R equi. Unstratified genotypic-phenotypic agreement for macrolides was fair (κ = 0.22 to 0.25). However, stratification by genomic copy number revealed near-perfect concordance (κ ≥ 0.97) exclusively among isolates harboring > 50,000 target copies. Alternative agents (gentamicin, ceftiofur, minocycline, doxycycline) maintained 97% to 100% susceptibility, regardless of erm(46) status. While erm(46) is widely distributed across R equi-endemic farms, actual phenotypic resistance expression is strongly copy-number dependent. The clinical emergence of erm(51) expands the known resistome of this pathogen. Incorporating quantitative molecular screening into routine R equi diagnostics provides crucial real-time therapeutic guidance, supporting precision medicine and targeted antimicrobial stewardship on endemic equine farms.

title: Antibiotic overuse and mortality in patients hospitalised for COVID-19: a global cohort study
abstract: Global antibiotic use during the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact remain unclear. This study analysed antibiotic use, bacterial co-infections, and the association between antibiotic use and in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalised for COVID-19, using a WHO database. We conducted a multicountry cohort study using anonymised patient-level data from The WHO Global Clinical Platform for COVID-19. Data were collected across 64 countries in all six WHO regions between January, 2020, and October, 2023. The study included hospitalised patients of all ages with suspected or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. We obtained patient-level data from standardised WHO case report forms completed prospectively or retrospectively and from harmonised national registries, research studies, and hospital databases. Patients without a suspected or confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or missing information on hospital admission date, antibiotic use, or outcome were excluded from the analysis. Patients were followed up from hospital admission until death, discharge, transfer, or 28 days, whichever occurred first. Follow-up data were collected at hospital discharge or death by the treating facility and entered into the platform. The primary outcome was 28-day in-hospital mortality, and we analysed this outcome using Cox proportional hazards models with a shared frailty term to account for country-level clustering. The median age of the study population was 61·9 years (±21·7), with 198 223 women and 251 990 men with data available on antibiotic use. Of the 592 898 patients enrolled, 451 291 (76·1%) had data on antibiotic use and were included in the descriptive analysis; 122 854 had complete data on empirical treatment type, of whom 47 359 (38·5%) were included in the regression analysis. Among the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use, 341 125 (75·6%) received antibiotics, more frequently in severe to critical cases than in mild to moderate cases (80·5% vs 71·6%). Prescribing was highest in the Eastern Mediterranean (83·0%) and African (82·7%) regions and lowest in the Western Pacific region (32·8%), declining in the European region and region of the Americas but increasing in the African region between 2020 and 2022. Treatment was predominantly empirical and involved Watch antibiotics of the WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve classification. Clinically suspected co-infections were reported in 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 patients; among those with positive cultures, 1815 (42·8%) of 4237 had multidrug-resistant bacteria. In the unadjusted analyses, empirical antibiotic use was associated with higher mortality across severity strata. After adjustment for age, sex, comorbidities, and disease severity, empirical antibiotic use remained associated with increased mortality in mild to moderate cases (adjusted hazard ratio 1·80, 95% CI 1·36-2·38) and severe to critical cases (1·16, 1·08-1·24). Despite clinically suspected co-infections being reported in only 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 enrolled patients, 341 125 (75·6%) of the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use received antibiotic therapy, predominantly broad-spectrum agents. As antibiotic use was not associated with improved clinical outcomes and is known to increase antimicrobial resistance, it should be rationalised through strengthened antimicrobial stewardship and behavioural interventions, particularly during respiratory viral epidemics. None.

title: Phylogeographical structure and genetic introgression in Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli: a genomic epidemiology study
abstract: Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli (S Napoli), a non-typhoidal Salmonella serotype that has been emerging in Italy, Switzerland, and France since the mid-1990s, has an unusual epidemiological profile that suggests a role for the environment in the transmission of these bacteria. The genomics of S Napoli has been inadequately characterised; we, therefore, aimed to provide a robust genomic framework for S Napoli surveillance. In this genomic epidemiology study, we performed short-read sequencing of 1145 S Napoli isolates from national surveillance in four European countries (Italy, Switzerland, France, and Spain) and complemented this dataset with 175 additional genomes (174 published and one unpublished). We used the EnteroBase core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme and its associated Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, along with other genome-based bioinformatics approaches such as single nucleotide variant-based phylogenetic analyses, ResFinder, PlasmidFinder, and RefSeq genomes, to characterise population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence, and differences in gene content among genetic lineages. We analysed 1320 S Napoli genomes, collected between April, 1945, and September 14, 2022, from human (n=1088, 82·4%) and non-human (n=232, 17·6%) sources in Italy (n=317, 24%), Switzerland (n=181, 13·7%), France (n=773, 58·5%), and Spain (n=48, 3·6%), confirming that the rising prevalence of S Napoli is driven by a single monophyletic serotype within cgMLST superlineage HC2000_1289. However, this serotype displays considerable genetic diversity (15 lineages falling into 12 HC900 clusters), strong spatial structuring, and a low frequency (2%) of AMR determinants. We also detected genetic introgression between S Napoli and the sympatric, closely related Salmonella enterica serotype Veneziana. Unlike successful non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes, for which globalisation has had a homogenising effect, S Napoli forms distinct lineages isolated by geographical distance. This study suggests that the persistence of S Napoli as a geographically structured metapopulation, causing localised human infections, could reflect the natural ecology of Salmonella before the rise of agribusiness. Future research should investigate the environmental reservoirs and transmission pathways of S Napoli.
